screens.title: Collider vs Rigidbody
screens.narratorSegment: A Collider is the shape Unity uses to detect contact or overlap; a Rigidbody is what lets the physics engine simulate mass, gravity, and forces. Put simply, the Collider answers the question "where" and the Rigidbody answers "how". Colliders alone can detect overlaps as static geometry, but without a Rigidbody there will be no physical response or OnCollisionEnter events for dynamic interactions. A common confusion is expecting collisions to produce forces when both objects only have Colliders. For a physical reaction—bounce, push, or knockback—at least one of the colliding objects must have a Rigidbody. Colliders come in several ready-made forms: BoxCollider, SphereCollider, CapsuleCollider, and the more costly MeshCollider used for complex meshes. Use simple colliders where possible for performance. In practice, assign a Collider to every interactive object, add a Rigidbody to the object that should be moved by physics, and cache the Rigidbody component in your script for efficient access. Example: a player character typically has a CapsuleCollider and a Rigidbody so that gravity, forces, and collision callbacks behave predictably. Misconception check: Colliders do not inherently move objects—Rigidbody does. Takeaway: decide whether the object must be simulated or only detected, then add the appropriate component.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Collider vs Rigidbody
Definition

Collider

Defines the physical boundary used for contact and overlap detection. Examples include Box, Sphere, Capsule, and Mesh colliders.

Use simple shapes
Prefer primitive colliders for performance.
Visualize in Scene
Green outlines help debug size and position.
Definition

Rigidbody

Adds mass, gravity, and response to forces. Required on at least one object for a collision to generate physical effects and OnCollision callbacks.

Best practice
Cache Rigidbody references in Start and apply forces through the Rigidbody API instead of setting transform.position for moving physics objects.
Example
Player (CapsuleCollider + Rigidbody) collides with Wall (BoxCollider). Because the player has a Rigidbody, OnCollisionEnter will fire and forces can be applied to bounce the player.
Common mistake
Expecting collisions to move objects when only Colliders are present. Add a Rigidbody to enable physical response.
Key takeaway
Choose Collider for shape, Rigidbody for motion. Together they provide predictable physics interactions.
Check your understanding
If two static colliders overlap without Rigidbodies, will OnCollisionEnter fire? Consider why or why not.

screens.title: Collider Types and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Unity provides several built-in collider types, each optimized for common shapes. BoxCollider and SphereCollider are inexpensive and perform well. CapsuleCollider is ideal for characters because it reduces snagging on corners. MeshCollider lets you match a complex model's shape closely, but it is significantly more expensive at runtime and can hurt performance if used excessively. When high fidelity is required, combine primitive colliders to approximate a complex model instead of relying on a MeshCollider everywhere. Another important detail is whether the MeshCollider is convex; convex mesh colliders allow for dynamic collisions with Rigidbodies, but non-convex mesh colliders are typically used for static environment geometry and cannot collide with dynamic mesh colliders. The choice of collider affects collision detection accuracy and C P U cost. A practical rule: favor simple primitives for frequent, moving objects and reserve complex mesh colliders for large, static geometry. Example: compose a car collision shape from multiple boxes and capsules rather than a full mesh for smoother physics and lower C P U overhead. Misconception check: more accurate colliders always mean better gameplay; in fact, performance and stable physics often benefit from simpler approximations. Takeaway: match collider shape to your performance and gameplay needs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Collider Types & Performance
Primitive colliders
  • BoxCollider: cheap and general-purpose.
  • SphereCollider: good for round objects and pickups.
  • CapsuleCollider: great for characters and smooth movement.
MeshCollider considerations

MeshColliders match a model's mesh but cost more CPU. Use convex mesh colliders for dynamic objects and non-convex for static scenery only.

Practical tip

Combine multiple primitives to approximate complex shapes for better performance and stable collisions.

Example
A racing car can use several BoxColliders and CapsuleColliders placed to approximate bumpers, wheels, and body panels. This keeps physics stable at high speeds compared to a single detailed mesh collider.
Warning
Avoid using many MeshColliders for moving objects; it will slow down collision checks and can cause unstable behavior.

screens.title: Collision Callbacks: OnCollisionEnter, Stay, Exit
screens.narratorSegment: When two colliders meet and at least one object has a Rigidbody, Unity triggers collision callbacks on scripts attached to those GameObjects. The primary methods are OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. OnCollisionEnter runs once at the start of the contact and provides a Collision parameter that includes contact points, normals, relative velocity, and a reference to the other collider. OnCollisionStay runs every physics frame while the contact persists, useful for grounding or continuous friction logic. OnCollisionExit runs once when objects separate. Using the Collision data you can compute the bounce direction by subtracting the other object's position from your position and normalizing the result, or you can read contact points to instantiate particles at the point of impact. A common example: when your player hits an obstacle tagged "Obstacle" you might compute a bounceDirection and call Rigidbody. AddForce(bounceDirection * bounceForce, ForceMode. Impulse). Misconception check: OnCollision callbacks will not fire if both colliders lack a Rigidbody or if a collider is marked as a trigger; verify the correct components and flags are set. Takeaway: use these callbacks and Collision details to implement physical responses and context-aware reactions during contact.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Collision Callbacks
Step-by-step
  1. OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision): single-frame event when contact begins. Inspect collision.gameObject and contact points.
  2. OnCollisionStay(Collision collision): called each physics update during contact; use for grounding checks.
  3. OnCollisionExit(Collision collision): called once when contact ends; useful to reset state.
What Collision contains
  • Contact points and normals
  • Reference to the other collider and GameObject
  • Relative velocity useful for damage or effects
Concrete example
If the player collides with an object tagged Obstacle, compute a bounce vector from collision.transform.position and call AddForce using ForceMode.Impulse on the player's Rigidbody to create an immediate push-back effect.
Key takeaway
Use Collision data to make informed physics responses and to place effects at accurate contact points.

screens.title: Triggers and the isTrigger Property
screens.narratorSegment: Triggers let you detect when another collider passes through or overlaps a collider without blocking movement or producing a physical response. You enable this behavior by checking Is Trigger on a Collider in the Inspector. Trigger callbacks are OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit, and they receive a Collider parameter rather than a Collision object because there are no contact points to report. Triggers are perfect for collectibles, area effects, and invisible zones—like a healing field or a checkpoint—that should respond when a player enters without stopping them. A common setup is to make coins have a SphereCollider with Is Trigger checked and no Rigidbody; when the player's Rigidbody enters the trigger, either the coin's or the player's script receives OnTriggerEnter and can verify the tag with CompareTag("Coin") before awarding points and calling Destroy(other. gameObject). Misconception check: OnTriggerEnter is not an alternative to OnCollisionEnter—it serves a different purpose. If you mark a collider as a trigger, OnCollisionEnter will not fire for that collider. Takeaway: use triggers for overlap detection and collisions for physical responses, and choose the appropriate callback for your gameplay need.

keyIdea.text: Set Is Trigger to detect overlaps with OnTrigger callbacks; triggers do not block movement.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Triggers & isTrigger
Trigger callbacks
  • OnTriggerEnter(Collider other): called once when another collider enters the trigger.
  • OnTriggerStay(Collider other): called every frame while an object remains inside.
  • OnTriggerExit(Collider other): called when the object leaves the trigger.
Practical coin example

Give a coin a SphereCollider with Is Trigger checked and no Rigidbody. When the player enters, check CompareTag("Coin"), increment score, and Destroy(other.gameObject).

Why use triggers
Triggers let you detect overlaps without interfering with movement, perfect for pickups, zones, and events tied to presence rather than physical impact.
Common pitfall
Trying to use OnCollisionEnter with a collider that has Is Trigger checked. Switch to OnTriggerEnter for triggers.

screens.title: Collision vs Trigger
screens.narratorSegment: Collisions and triggers both involve colliders, but they serve different purposes. Collisions are physical: if two colliders meet and at least one has a Rigidbody, physical response, contact points, and OnCollision callbacks are available. Triggers are non-physical: a collider set to Is Trigger reports overlaps via OnTrigger callbacks and does not block motion. Think in terms of gameplay intent: use collisions when you want the engine to resolve intersections naturally — for example, preventing the player from walking through walls, applying knock-back, or stopping a projectile. Use triggers when you want to detect presence without obstructing movement — for example, a collectible, a zone that heals the player, or an invisible checkpoint. A concrete example: a coin should be a trigger so the player picks it up without interruption, while a wall should be a collider so it prevents passage. Misconception check: marking a collider as a trigger does not retain contact point information; you should not expect Collision data in a trigger. Takeaway: pick the interaction type that matches whether objects should be physically blocked or simply observed, and implement the corresponding callback methods.

Collision (physical)
  • Requires Collider on both and at least one Rigidbody
  • Produces OnCollisionEnter/Stay/Exit with Collision data
  • Blocks movement and produces physical response
Trigger (overlap)
  • Set Is Trigger on a Collider
  • Uses OnTriggerEnter/Stay/Exit with a Collider parameter
  • Does not block movement—ideal for pickups and zones
Example
Coins are triggers; walls are colliders. This preserves player movement while detecting collections.
Misconception
A trigger still requires a Collider component; it simply switches the response mode to overlap reporting.

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a compact C# script pattern that handles both collisions and triggers. The script caches a Rigidbody reference in Start and then implements OnCollisionEnter to detect physical impacts and OnTriggerEnter to detect pick-ups. In OnCollisionEnter we check the collided object's tag, compute a bounce direction from positions, and call rb. AddForce with ForceMode. Impulse to push the player. In OnTriggerEnter we use CompareTag to recognize coins and power-ups, increment a score, and call Destroy on the other. gameObject. This pattern keeps logic clear: collision responses use Collision data for physics reactions while triggers use Collider to process overlap events. A practical note: cache components like Rigidbody in Start to avoid expensive GetComponent calls during collisions. Also, ensure the objects' tags and collider settings in the Inspector match what the script expects. Misconception check: do not expect OnCollisionEnter to run for a trigger collider—these methods are distinct. Takeaway: keep collision and trigger logic separate, test using the Console messages, and tweak bounceForce to feel right for your game. In practical terms, a practical script for bouncing and collecting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › PlayerCollisionHandler.cs
Code example
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerCollisionHandler : MonoBehaviour
{
    public int score = 0;
    public float bounceForce = 500f;

    private Rigidbody rb;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
        if (rb == null)
        {
            Debug.LogWarning("PlayerCollisionHandler on " + gameObject.name + " requires a Rigidbody for physics interactions.");
        }
    }

    void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
    {
        if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Obstacle"))
        {
            Vector3 bounceDirection = (transform.position - collision.transform.position).normalized;
            if (rb != null)
            {
                rb.AddForce(bounceDirection * bounceForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
            }
        }
    }

    void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        if (other.CompareTag("Coin"))
        {
            score += 10;
            Debug.Log("Collected a coin! Score: " + score);
            Destroy(other.gameObject);
        }
    }
}
Quick notes
  • Escape angle using positions to compute bounceDirection.
  • Use CompareTag for efficient tag checks.
  • Destroy the trigger object when collected to remove it from the scene.
Example scenario
Attach this script to the Player (Capsule) with a Rigidbody and CapsuleCollider. Create Coins with SphereCollider set to Is Trigger and tag Coin.
Key Takeaway
Separate collision and trigger logic, cache components, and verify inspector settings for tags and collider flags.

screens.title: Layer Filtering and Collision Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: Not every object should interact with every other object. Unity's Layer system and the Layer Collision Matrix permit selective collision rules. Assign GameObjects to layers in the Inspector, then open Edit → Project Settings → Physics and use the Matrix to enable or disable collisions between layers. This is powerful for both gameplay and performance: for example, make player bullets ignore friendly characters by removing collisions between the Bullet and Friendly layers. Filtering with layers reduces the number of collision checks the physics engine performs, lowering C P U load and reducing noisy event logic. Use layers combined with CompareTag when you need both fast filtering and precise identification in code. A concrete workflow: create layers for Player, Enemy, Bullet, and Environment, then disable Bullet-to-Bullet and Bullet-to-Player collisions if appropriate. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Layer Filtering
Why layers matter

Layers let you specify which categories of objects should detect collisions with each other. Use the Layer Collision Matrix in Project Settings to turn interactions on or off between pairs of layers.

Practical setup
  1. Create layers (Player, Enemy, Bullet, Environment).
  2. Assign GameObjects to their layers in the Inspector.
  3. Open Physics settings and uncheck interactions you want disabled.
Example
Disable Bullet-to-Bullet collisions and Bullet-to-Friendly collisions by unchecking those boxes in the Layer Collision Matrix. This prevents unnecessary collisions and simplifies logic.
Tip
Use layers for bulk filtering and CompareTag in scripts for fine-grained identification after a collision or trigger fires.

screens.title: Lab: Collectible System Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: In this lab you'll create a collectible system where the player collects coins and gains points. Start by placing a Plane for the ground and a Capsule for the Player. Add a Rigidbody and a CapsuleCollider to the player and ensure freezeRotation if you don't want tumbling. For each coin, use a Sphere with a SphereCollider and check Is Trigger; do not add a Rigidbody unless you want the coin to be affected by physics. Tag each coin as Coin. Create a PlayerInteraction script that caches the player's Rigidbody and contains OnTriggerEnter(Collider other). In that method use other. CompareTag("Coin") to confirm the collider is a coin, increment an integer score, print the score to the Console, and call Destroy(other. gameObject) to remove the coin. Run the game and walk over coins; they should disappear and the score should increase. If OnTriggerEnter doesn't run, verify that the player has a Rigidbody and at least one collider and that the coin's collider has Is Trigger enabled. Misconception check: triggers require a Collider on the other object; both sides need a collider but only one needs a Rigidbody for proper detection in many setups. Takeaway: small inspector misconfigurations are the usual reason triggers fail, so check colliders, Rigidbody, and tag names.

screens.title: Common Setup Mistakes and Debugging
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners frequently face a few recurring issues when working with collisions and triggers. The top mistake is expecting OnCollisionEnter to fire when no Rigidbody is present. Remember: Colliders alone may overlap, but without a Rigidbody there is no physical collision response and those callbacks might not fire as expected. Another pitfall is mixing trigger and collision methods: a collider set to Is Trigger will not call OnCollisionEnter; use the trigger callbacks instead. Collider sizing and positioning also cause problems—small or misplaced colliders won't overlap the way you expect. Visualize colliders in the Scene view to confirm alignment. For fast-moving objects, a second class of problems appears: tunneling, where an object moves through another between physics steps. Use Continuous collision detection modes or adjust physics settings to reduce tunneling. When physics-driven movement is required, avoid directly setting transform. position; instead use Rigidbody. velocity or Rigidbody. AddForce, which respects collisions and the physics solver. Debugging steps: log messages in callbacks, visualize colliders, check Rigidbody presence, and verify tag strings used with CompareTag. Takeaway: most issues are configuration errors; a quick inspector and Scene-view check often reveals the cause.

Checklist to fix event failures
  • Is there a Rigidbody on at least one object?
  • Is the collider marked Is Trigger when expecting trigger events?
  • Are collider sizes and positions correct (use Scene visualization)?
Tunneling & movement

For fast objects, set Collision Detection to Continuous or Continuous Dynamic on the Rigidbody, and move objects with physics APIs rather than directly setting transform.position to prevent passing through colliders.

Debug tip
Insert Debug.Log statements in your callback methods to confirm whether they fire, and check tag names for typos when using CompareTag.
Key takeaway
Most problems are configuration errors. Verify components, flags, and scene visualization before changing code.

screens.title: Physics-driven Movement and Moving Platforms
screens.narratorSegment: When interacting with moving platforms or fast objects, follow two patterns for stable physics. First, move physics objects using Rigidbody methods—set Rigidbody. velocity or call Rigidbody. AddForce—instead of directly modifying transform. position. Directly setting transform can bypass the physics solver and cause tunneling or jitter. Second, for players standing on moving platforms, a robust solution is to temporarily make the player a child of the platform transform while contact persists. Detect when the player lands on the platform using OnCollisionEnter and set transform. parent to the platform; on OnCollisionExit set parent back to null. This ensures the player moves exactly with the platform, avoiding sliding or falling due to physics rounding. For tunneling issues with very fast objects, change the Rigidbody's Collision Detection mode from Discrete to Continuous or Continuous Dynamic to increase detection rigor. Misconception check: parenting the player to the platform is not a physics hack; it's a practical way to guarantee visual and positional consistency when platforms are kinematic or controlled by animation or script. Takeaway: combine physics-friendly movement and smart parenting to keep interactions stable and predictable.

Move with physics

Use Rigidbody.velocity or AddForce to move objects so collisions and continuous contact are handled by the physics solver.

Parenting to platforms

When the player lands on a kinematic or scripted platform, set transform.parent to the platform to ensure consistent movement, and remove the parent when the player leaves.

Switch Rigidbody Collision Detection to Continuous or Continuous Dynamic for fast-moving objects to reduce passing through colliders between frames.

Prefer physics APIs for movement and use parenting for platform adherence to maintain stable gameplay feel.

fullNarratorScript:
In 3D games, interactions—like bumping into walls, picking up coins, or being knocked back by an enemy—are handled by Unity's physics system. This lesson focuses on two core building blocks: Colliders, which define the shape or hitbox of a GameObject, and Rigidbodies, which give an object mass and allow it to be simulated by the physics engine. You'll learn the practical difference between a collision event and a trigger event, how to use the common callback methods in C#, and the simple rules that decide whether Unity will physically respond to two objects. We'll also walk through a real example: a player collecting a coin using a trigger, and being pushed back by an enemy with a Rigidbody. By mastering these pieces you'll avoid typical beginner mistakes—like expecting OnCollisionEnter to fire when both objects only have colliders but no Rigidbody—and you'll be able to design efficient, reliable collision behavior. Think about one interaction you want in your game, and keep that scenario in mind as we unpack the components and methods you'll use.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish between a Collider and a Rigidbody, implement collision and trigger callbacks in C#, configure trigger colliders for overlap detection, and apply simple physics responses such as adding force or destroying objects on impact. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: first, recognizing which component controls shape and which controls physics; second, writing and using OnCollisionEnter and OnTriggerEnter to respond to events; third, using the isTrigger property to switch a collider from blocking to reporting overlaps; and fourth, avoiding common setup mistakes like missing Rigidbodies or using transform. position for physics-driven movement. These skills matter because correct setup determines whether Unity will register events at all and whether interactions behave predictably. For example, you'll be able to set up a coin that disappears when collected, and an enemy that applies a knock-back force when hit. Each objective includes a small verification milestone so you can check that your scene responds correctly under test conditions.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical lab outcomes: build a collectible that disappears on overlap, add an enemy that physically pushes the player, and test layer filtering to prevent unwanted interactions. You will write OnTriggerEnter to detect coins and destroy them, using CompareTag to identify the coin reliably. You will also implement OnCollisionEnter to respond to an enemy collision, calculating a bounce direction and applying an impulse via Rigidbody. AddForce. Finally, you will test scene behavior under different layer settings and confirm that the Layer Collision Matrix prevents collisions you explicitly disable. These tasks emphasize reproducible tests: verify score increases when collecting a coin, and confirm the player's Rigidbody receives a force when hit by an enemy. Why this matters: hands-on verification ensures your logic runs in the same way the physics engine will evaluate it at runtime. If you complete these objectives, you will be ready to avoid the most common setup issues and create predictable interaction behaviors in your game.

A Collider is the shape Unity uses to detect contact or overlap; a Rigidbody is what lets the physics engine simulate mass, gravity, and forces. Put simply, the Collider answers the question "where" and the Rigidbody answers "how". Colliders alone can detect overlaps as static geometry, but without a Rigidbody there will be no physical response or OnCollisionEnter events for dynamic interactions. A common confusion is expecting collisions to produce forces when both objects only have Colliders. For a physical reaction—bounce, push, or knockback—at least one of the colliding objects must have a Rigidbody. Colliders come in several ready-made forms: BoxCollider, SphereCollider, CapsuleCollider, and the more costly MeshCollider used for complex meshes. Use simple colliders where possible for performance. In practice, assign a Collider to every interactive object, add a Rigidbody to the object that should be moved by physics, and cache the Rigidbody component in your script for efficient access. Example: a player character typically has a CapsuleCollider and a Rigidbody so that gravity, forces, and collision callbacks behave predictably. Misconception check: Colliders do not inherently move objects—Rigidbody does. Takeaway: decide whether the object must be simulated or only detected, then add the appropriate component.

Unity provides several built-in collider types, each optimized for common shapes. BoxCollider and SphereCollider are inexpensive and perform well. CapsuleCollider is ideal for characters because it reduces snagging on corners. MeshCollider lets you match a complex model's shape closely, but it is significantly more expensive at runtime and can hurt performance if used excessively. When high fidelity is required, combine primitive colliders to approximate a complex model instead of relying on a MeshCollider everywhere. Another important detail is whether the MeshCollider is convex; convex mesh colliders allow for dynamic collisions with Rigidbodies, but non-convex mesh colliders are typically used for static environment geometry and cannot collide with dynamic mesh colliders. The choice of collider affects collision detection accuracy and C P U cost. A practical rule: favor simple primitives for frequent, moving objects and reserve complex mesh colliders for large, static geometry. Example: compose a car collision shape from multiple boxes and capsules rather than a full mesh for smoother physics and lower C P U overhead. Misconception check: more accurate colliders always mean better gameplay; in fact, performance and stable physics often benefit from simpler approximations. Takeaway: match collider shape to your performance and gameplay needs.

When two colliders meet and at least one object has a Rigidbody, Unity triggers collision callbacks on scripts attached to those GameObjects. The primary methods are OnCollisionEnter, OnCollisionStay, and OnCollisionExit. OnCollisionEnter runs once at the start of the contact and provides a Collision parameter that includes contact points, normals, relative velocity, and a reference to the other collider. OnCollisionStay runs every physics frame while the contact persists, useful for grounding or continuous friction logic. OnCollisionExit runs once when objects separate. Using the Collision data you can compute the bounce direction by subtracting the other object's position from your position and normalizing the result, or you can read contact points to instantiate particles at the point of impact. A common example: when your player hits an obstacle tagged "Obstacle" you might compute a bounceDirection and call Rigidbody. AddForce(bounceDirection * bounceForce, ForceMode. Impulse). Misconception check: OnCollision callbacks will not fire if both colliders lack a Rigidbody or if a collider is marked as a trigger; verify the correct components and flags are set. Takeaway: use these callbacks and Collision details to implement physical responses and context-aware reactions during contact.

Triggers let you detect when another collider passes through or overlaps a collider without blocking movement or producing a physical response. You enable this behavior by checking Is Trigger on a Collider in the Inspector. Trigger callbacks are OnTriggerEnter, OnTriggerStay, and OnTriggerExit, and they receive a Collider parameter rather than a Collision object because there are no contact points to report. Triggers are perfect for collectibles, area effects, and invisible zones—like a healing field or a checkpoint—that should respond when a player enters without stopping them. A common setup is to make coins have a SphereCollider with Is Trigger checked and no Rigidbody; when the player's Rigidbody enters the trigger, either the coin's or the player's script receives OnTriggerEnter and can verify the tag with CompareTag("Coin") before awarding points and calling Destroy(other. gameObject). Misconception check: OnTriggerEnter is not an alternative to OnCollisionEnter—it serves a different purpose. If you mark a collider as a trigger, OnCollisionEnter will not fire for that collider. Takeaway: use triggers for overlap detection and collisions for physical responses, and choose the appropriate callback for your gameplay need.

Collisions and triggers both involve colliders, but they serve different purposes. Collisions are physical: if two colliders meet and at least one has a Rigidbody, physical response, contact points, and OnCollision callbacks are available. Triggers are non-physical: a collider set to Is Trigger reports overlaps via OnTrigger callbacks and does not block motion. Think in terms of gameplay intent: use collisions when you want the engine to resolve intersections naturally — for example, preventing the player from walking through walls, applying knock-back, or stopping a projectile. Use triggers when you want to detect presence without obstructing movement — for example, a collectible, a zone that heals the player, or an invisible checkpoint. A concrete example: a coin should be a trigger so the player picks it up without interruption, while a wall should be a collider so it prevents passage. Misconception check: marking a collider as a trigger does not retain contact point information; you should not expect Collision data in a trigger. Takeaway: pick the interaction type that matches whether objects should be physically blocked or simply observed, and implement the corresponding callback methods.

AddForce—instead of directly modifying transform. position. Directly setting transform can bypass the physics solver and cause tunneling or jitter. Second, for players standing on moving platforms, a robust solution is to temporarily make the player a child of the platform transform while contact persists. Detect when the player lands on the platform using OnCollisionEnter and set transform. parent to the platform; on OnCollisionExit set parent back to null. This ensures the player moves exactly with the platform, avoiding sliding or falling due to physics rounding. For tunneling issues with very fast objects, change the Rigidbody's Collision Detection mode from Discrete to Continuous or Continuous Dynamic to increase detection rigor. Misconception check: parenting the player to the platform is not a physics hack; it's a practical way to guarantee visual and positional consistency when platforms are kinematic or controlled by animation or script. Takeaway: combine physics-friendly movement and smart parenting to keep interactions stable and predictable.

Let's review the essential ideas you should carry forward. First, Colliders define the detection shape while Rigidbodies enable physics simulation; both have distinct responsibilities. Second, use collision callbacks when you need physical response and access to contact data, and use trigger callbacks when you only need to know that something overlapped your zone. Third, prefer simple primitive colliders for moving objects and use the Layer Collision Matrix to efficiently filter interactions. Finally, avoid common mistakes: check Rigidbody presence, don't confuse OnCollisionEnter with OnTriggerEnter, move physics objects with Rigidbody APIs, and consider continuous collision detection or parenting when objects move quickly or when platforms need to carry the player. These patterns together let you build reliable, performant interactions in your game scenes.
